interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — Pluxee N.V. (PLX.PA, Euronext Paris)

*Prepared 2026-07-17. Price used throughout: **EUR 13.76** (Euronext Paris close, 2026-07-16, via FMP live quote). All figures in euros unless stated. Pluxee's fiscal year ends 31 August, so "H1 fiscal 2026" means September 2025 through February 2026, and "Q3 fiscal 2026" means March through May 2026.*

Pluxee is the employee-benefits business Sodexo spun off and listed separately in February 2024. It issues meal and lifestyle vouchers (increasingly digital cards and an app) that employers buy for their staff, and it earns money three ways: a fee from the employer, a commission from the merchant who accepts the voucher, and interest on the large pool of client money it holds between issuing a voucher and paying the merchant — what the industry calls the "float". It operates in 28 countries; Latin America (overwhelmingly Brazil) and Continental Europe are roughly 40% and 44% of operating revenue.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

**The story has quietly changed shape over the last nine months, from "low-double-digit growth compounder" to "cost and cash machine absorbing a regulatory reset."**

At the fiscal 2025 results call (30 October 2025), the framing was unambiguously offensive. Aurélien Sonet led with "another very strong year, in which we executed our strategy with discipline and delivered above expectations across all key metrics" — 10.6% organic revenue growth, recurring earnings margin up 230 basis points against a 150-point plan, 89% cash conversion against a target of "above 75%". The capital-allocation news was a flex, not a defence: a raised dividend of EUR 0.38 per share plus a first-ever EUR 100 million buyback, which the CFO explicitly tied to the share price — "we are aware of where the stock price is currently trading, and versus the value we consider we are able to create from this company."

Thirteen days later, on 12 November 2025, the Brazilian government issued the decree reforming the PAT (Programa de Alimentação do Trabalhador — the tax-favoured meal-benefit scheme that is the economic basis of Pluxee's largest market). Pluxee cut its fiscal 2026 guidance on 17 November 2025. That single external event is the hinge of the whole arc.

By the H1 fiscal 2026 call (16 April 2026), the vocabulary had inverted. Growth was no longer the lead — margin was: "profitability delivered ahead of plan", "operating leverage embedded in our business model", "the strong execution of our efficiency initiatives", "cost discipline has become an increasingly important margin driver". Organic revenue growth had halved to 5.6%. The agenda itself now carried a dedicated item — "an update on the regulatory situation in Brazil" — that did not exist a year earlier.

Two growth drivers were quietly demoted along the way. **Public Benefits** (state-funded programmes) went from a proof point in October 2025 to a euphemism by April 2026 — "the effects related to the contract cycle and order phasing, which are inherent in this business" — after the CFO had already conceded in October that "some countries, especially in Western Europe, like Romania or Austria... decisions were taken by the state, and because of some budget constraints, to suspend or to reduce some of these programs." **Net retention** slid from a headline achievement ("we maintained a net retention rate of 100%, in line with our midterm objective") to a hedge ("net retention proved resilient despite a more challenging macro environment"), and by Q3 fiscal 2026 it had printed **99%** — below the stated above-100% objective.

Two drivers were promoted to carry the load: **face value increases** (legal caps on voucher values rising across Europe, plus Latin American inflation) and **acquisitions** (Beneficio Fácil, Cobee, Skipr, the Santander partnership). Both are real. Both are also, notably, drivers that do not require the underlying employed population to grow — which matters, because that is precisely what stopped growing.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

**Before the table, three corrections to the screener block that the director must see, because two of them invert the headline conclusion.**

| Screener field | What it says | What is actually true | Why it is wrong |
|---|---|---|---|
| **TTM diluted EPS** | **2.53** | **≈ 1.42** | Pluxee reports semi-annually. The data feed labels those half-year periods "Q2" and "Q4", so summing "four quarters" (0.73 + 0.69 + 0.67 + 0.44) sums **two full years**. Real trailing-twelve-month earnings per share = H2 fiscal 2025 (0.69) + H1 fiscal 2026 (0.73) = **1.42**. |
| **TTM FCF 540M** | 540M | **≈ 417M** (fiscal 2025 recurring free cash flow, company-reported); H1 fiscal 2026 recurring free cash flow was 210M | Same double-count mechanic. Management's own figure: "our free cash flow engine has expanded very materially from circa EUR 290 million in fiscal 2023 to EUR 417 million in fiscal 2025." |
| **Net cash 2.02B** ("a genuine SoP add-back") | 2.02B | Company-reported **net financial cash of ~1.27B** at 28 February 2026 — and only a *minority slice* of that is genuinely free | This is the single most important correction. Most of Pluxee's cash is **float** — money that belongs to clients and is owed to merchants. Management draws the line themselves: "it's worth differentiating 2 cash position. You have the overall net cash position. And we also disclosed... what we call this net excess cash position, making a clear distinction between the contribution of float related cash to cash and this excess cash." They then showed the two moving in *opposite* directions in H1 fiscal 2026: "this EUR 107 million improvement in the overall net cash position is the combination of EUR 140 million **decrease in excess cash** and EUR 240 million improvement overall on the float related [position]." Treating 2.02B as a shareholder add-back would count client money twice — once as cash on the balance sheet and again as the float interest income capitalised in the earnings multiple. |

Knock-on: the screener's "Fair Value 25.34 / Margin of Safety 104%", "DCF fair value 77.7" and "P/FCF 5.8x" are all computed off the doubled earnings and cash-flow base. **They are artefacts, not signals.** The Altman-Z of 0.9 is equally meaningless here — a solvency score built for manufacturers reads a benefits company's client float as crushing current liabilities.

**Now the claims themselves.**

| Management claim | Where | The hard evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Robust margin expansion... underscoring the operating leverage of our model" | FY25 + H1 FY26 | Recurring earnings margin +230bp in fiscal 2025 (vs +150bp planned), then +229bp organically in H1 fiscal 2026 to 37%; recurring earnings +12.9% organic on +5.6% revenue. Reported net income 68M (H2 FY24) → 100M (H2 FY25) → 105M (H1 FY26). | **Corroborated.** The strongest, cleanest claim in the file. |
| "Outstanding cash generation and conversion" | FY25 | 89% recurring cash conversion vs a ">75% average" target; 86% in H1 fiscal 2026; free cash flow 290M (FY23) → 417M (FY25). | **Corroborated**, once the feed's doubled 540M is discarded. |
| "Strong momentum in new client acquisition" | Every call | EUR 1.5B of new annualised business volume in fiscal 2025 vs a 1.3B target; a record 0.9B in H1 fiscal 2026; 1.2B by Q3 = 92% of the full-year target with a quarter to run; business volume issued +9.4% organic in Q3 fiscal 2026. | **Corroborated — and this is the tell.** Volumes are *growing high-single-digit while revenue shrinks*. The problem is not demand. It is price, imposed by regulators. |
| "We maintained a net retention rate of 100%, in line with our midterm objective" | FY25 | Printed **99% in Q3 fiscal 2026** — below the above-100% target. The CEO had already conceded the cause: end-user portfolio contribution "turned negative" in H2 fiscal 2025. | **Diverging.** Not yet broken, but the claim has lapsed and the driver is deteriorating, not stabilising. |
| "Consensus fwd EPS growth +0.4%" (screener) vs "we remain deeply committed to establishing Pluxee as a sustainably profitable growth group" | FY25 close | The street models roughly flat earnings. Q3 fiscal 2026 organic revenue **−3.3%**; management guides Q4's Brazil drag at "twice the impact that we had in Q3". | **Narrative is richer than the trajectory.** The words still say growth compounder; the numbers say two years of flat-to-down revenue while a regulator resets the take rate. |
| "Beat 1 of 5 quarters (20%)" (screener) | — | Against *revenue* consensus Pluxee has been closer than that: Q3 fiscal 2026 revenue of 312M beat the ~299M consensus and organic −3.3% beat the −4.3% feared (3 July 2026). | **Screener metric is unreliable for a semi-annual reporter** and should not be leaned on. |

**The core forensic finding:** the operational claims are true and the accounting is clean. What is *not* true is the screener's premise that this is a 5.8x free-cash-flow, 104%-margin-of-safety orphan. Strip the double-count and the float, and Pluxee is a well-run, modestly-levered duopolist whose regulator is legislating its take rate down — trading at a *modest*, not spectacular, discount.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Declining** — from confident-offensive to confident-defensive. The confidence is intact; the *subject* of the confidence has moved from revenue to costs.

- **FY25 (30 Oct 2025) — offensive.** "Delivered above expectations across all key metrics"; "we are clearly well ahead of our initial plan"; "a step change in the group's financial profile". Even the buyback was framed as conviction: "this is a very good sign of our confidence in the Pluxee potential."
- **FY25, under questioning — the first crack.** Pressed by Barclays on the Q4 slowdown, the CFO named it: state programmes "suspend[ed] or... reduce[d]" in Romania and Austria, "weighing at least temporarily, and we'll see further on our organic growth." That "we'll see further" is the only unhedged moment of uncertainty in the October call.
- **H1 FY26 (16 Apr 2026) — defensive, but specific.** "Solid", "resilient", "on track" replace "outstanding" and "above expectations". The framing is explicitly about withstanding: "allows us to enter H2 from a position of strength amid a more uncertain macro and geopolitical environment."
- **H1 FY26, the Brazil answer — the most important tonal moment.** Asked by UBS whether the reiterated earnings guidance implied conservatism, the CFO instead pre-announced a decline: "we expect all the regions to go on improving the EBITDA margin... with one exception, one big exception, which is going to be Brazil... the reform for the short term and for the second half of the year will weigh a lot on the EBITDA margin of the group... in the second half of the year, we will face a lower EBITDA margin compared to the previous year." That is a management team walking *toward* the bad news, unprompted, on the record. It is a credibility asset.
- **Q3 FY26 (3 Jul 2026) — clinical.** Guidance confirmed; the Q4 hit quantified in advance ("twice the impact that we had in Q3"); fiscal 2027 guidance explicitly withheld as "too early".

Guidance has become *more* specific over time, not less — the opposite of the usual deterioration pattern. But specificity is now being spent describing decline.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High.**

| Guided | When | Delivered | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Low double-digit" organic revenue growth, FY25 | FY24 | +10.6% organic | Met |
| ~+150bp recurring margin expansion, FY25 | FY24 | **+230bp** | Beat materially |
| ">75% average" cash conversion, FY24–26 | FY24 | 89% (FY25), 86% (H1 FY26) | Beat, then *raised* the commitment to ">80% average" |
| EUR 1.3B annual new-client business volume | FY25 | EUR 1.5B | Beat |
| EUR 3B cumulative face-value uplift over 3 years | FY24 | 2.9B reached by H1 FY26 (year 2 of 3) | On track / early |
| FY26 objectives *as revised 17 Nov 2025* (stable organic revenue, slight margin expansion, ~80% cash conversion) | Nov 2025 | Confirmed at H1 (Apr) and again at Q3 (Jul); 9-month revenue +2.7% organic | Tracking |

**No sandbagging pattern in the ordinary sense — the reverse.** They set a 150bp margin target and delivered 230bp, then raised the cash-conversion floor rather than bank the beat. The one guidance cut (17 November 2025) came **five days** after the Brazilian decree — immediate, not delayed, not drip-fed. When they had a chance to hide behind "conservatism" on the April call, they instead volunteered that H2 group margin would fall.

The screener's "beat 1/5 quarters (20%)" contradicts this and should be disregarded: Pluxee reports twice a year and gives revenue-only updates in Q1/Q3, so a quarterly EPS-beat count is measuring noise. The Q3 fiscal 2026 print (3 July 2026) beat both revenue and organic-growth consensus.

**One genuine reservation:** the fiscal 2027 guide has been deferred. Management called it "too early to provide detailed fiscal 2027 guidance" given "ongoing regulatory uncertainty". Their credibility is high *on things they have guided*. The number that matters most to the stock right now is the one they have not yet given.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **"What are you doing with the cash?" — asked repeatedly, never fully answered.** Deutsche Bank's André Juillard (H1 FY26): "Your cash net position is even stronger than what it was at the end of last year. Do you have any new plan about the use of this cash or still not clear?" The answer was the float/excess-cash distinction plus "M&A remains a key pillar... we'll come back to you when it will be." The same analyst had already needled them in October — "as a summary, the message is step by step" — and the CFO's reply, "As always," is the tell. **Analysts do not believe the cash pile is as available as it looks, and management has not shown them the excess-cash bridge in a way that settles it.** This is the pressure point that later turned into the buyback.
- **Net retention decomposition — deflected twice.** Bernstein's Sabrina Blanc pushed on where retention deteriorated; the answer named "the evolution of the end user portfolio" but gave no numbers. She then asked directly for the non-meal-voucher share of revenue and got only: "the contribution coming from the cross-selling in percentage is higher than the overall growth." **A ratio in place of a number.** The multi-benefit diversification story — the strategic answer to meal-voucher regulatory risk — is unquantified.
- **The Q4 fiscal 2025 order postponement — asked, answered vaguely, then confirmed as real.** Barclays' Pravin Gondhale asked for the size of the postponed European public programmes. The CFO: "I don't have in mind the impact in terms of basis points." Six months later Public Benefits weakness in Continental Europe was a named drag, and by Q3 fiscal 2026 Continental Europe operating revenue was **−1.5% over nine months**. The non-answer preceded the bad news.
- **The AI question analysts are asking and management cannot answer.** UBS's Mahir Bidani (H1 FY26) asked whether client headcount reductions were "because of AI fears and then stopping hiring". The CEO's answer was candid to a fault: "most of them are wondering what would be the future of their organization. **Not many of them have very clear answers.**" He then named automotive, IT and staffing as under pressure. **Pluxee's revenue is a levered bet on the number of employed people at its clients** — and it has just told the market that its clients do not know what that number will be.
- **What analysts are not pressing on, and should be: interoperability.** The Brazil discussion is framed as a merchant-fee cap and payment terms. The 12 November 2026 milestone — full interoperability, forcing the closed-loop network open — is the leg that attacks the *moat*, not the margin. It gets far less airtime than the 3.6% fee cap.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The take rate is being legislated down.** Brazil's PAT reform capped the merchant discount rate at 3.6% (effective 10 February 2026), imposed 15-day merchant reimbursement, opened the system to a 2% interchange arrangement (11 May 2026) and mandates full interoperability from 12 November 2026. Group take-up rate is already down ~50 basis points. Management's own 4-year brag — "we have improved our take rate of 50 basis points" over four years (FY25 call) — has been erased by one decree.

🔴 **Volumes up, revenue down — the definition of price destruction.** Q3 fiscal 2026: business volume issued **+9.4%** organic, Employee Benefits volume **+8.0%**, and total revenue **−3.3%** organic. The engine is running; the meter has been re-geared.

🔴 **Net retention broke below the objective** — 99% in Q3 fiscal 2026 against an above-100% target, with the CEO attributing it to end-user portfolios that "turned negative" (H2 fiscal 2025) and to clients in automotive, IT and staffing "reading [reducing] some of their budgets".

🔴 **The worst quarter is still ahead and pre-announced.** "In Q4, the impact will be somehow, in term of organic growth, twice the impact that we had in Q3 for Brazil" (CFO, 3 July 2026). Fiscal 2027 guidance withheld.

🔴 **The cash is not what the screen thinks it is.** See §2. Excess cash *fell* EUR 140 million in H1 fiscal 2026.

🔴 **Insider buy ratio 0.00** — while the *company* bought EUR 100 million of stock, no individual insider did.

🟢 **Management pre-announced its own bad news, twice.** Guidance cut five days after the Brazilian decree (17 November 2025); H2 margin decline volunteered in answer to a question about *conservatism* (16 April 2026). This is not a promotional team.

🟢 **Margin expansion is structural, not cosmetic** — +230bp (FY25) and +229bp organic (H1 FY26), sourced to platform consolidation, product-range streamlining and automation, and delivered while revenue growth halved. The efficiency programme is doing exactly what it claimed.

🟢 **Commercial engine is genuinely strong** — 92% of the full-year new-client target achieved with a quarter remaining; small-business acquisition now >30% of new business, which is the mix that historically carries a better take rate.

🟢 **Brazil came in less bad than feared** — Q3 organic −3.3% vs −4.3% consensus, revenue 312M vs ~299M expected; shares +6% on 3 July 2026.

🟢 **Geographic and driver diversification is real** — 28 countries, three regions, face-value legal-cap increases across Europe providing a mechanical volume tailwind independent of employment.

🟢 **The capital-allocation policy moved from words to cash** — first buyback (EUR 100 million) plus a 9% dividend increase, with the CFO explicitly anchoring it to the depressed share price.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **The float/excess-cash distinction is now volunteered, not extracted.** In October 2025 the cash story was "significant increases in our net cash position". By April 2026 the CFO opens with "it's worth differentiating 2 cash position" *before* being pressed. **Management is pre-emptively deflating a balance-sheet number the market was over-reading.** When a CFO volunteers that his cash is smaller than it looks, believe him — and note that the screener's 2.02B add-back is exactly the error he is trying to head off.
- **"Sustainably profitable growth group" replaced "low double-digit growth".** In October 2025 the objective was a number. By April 2026 the closing line is an adjective. The quantified ambition has been retired without ever being formally withdrawn.
- **A new voice with a different register.** The Q3 fiscal 2026 call (3 July 2026) was fronted on the Brazil question by CFO **Stéphane Abrioux**, not Stéphane Lhopiteau. The tonal shift is notable: where Lhopiteau spent paragraphs contextualising, Abrioux quantified the coming damage in one sentence — "twice the impact that we had in Q3". A cleaner, colder communication style, which usually accompanies an internal decision to stop defending the old growth frame.
- **"Highly selective" is doing quiet work.** Public Benefits is now always accompanied by "our highly selective approach" and "sustainably accretive to growth and profitability" — the language of a business being shrunk on purpose, pre-justified. Same with the UK and US: "progressively exiting noncore, lower return activities", "less than 5% of group revenues", "should return to a positive contribution from fiscal 2027". Three separate revenue lines have been pre-excused.
- **Interoperability is being discussed as a payments feature, not as the end of the moat.** The FY25 call sells payment-agnosticism as a *strength* — "being fully payment agnostic, it integrates the most popular digital payment options such as Google Pay, Apple Pay, and QR code solutions". That is the same force Brazil is about to mandate. When the closed loop is opened by law, the merchant network — the thing that makes a Pluxee card worth more to an employer than a bank card — becomes contestable by any card issuer. **Management frames this as convenience. It is the moat.**
- **AI appears on both sides of the ledger, and management only counts one.** AI is repeatedly claimed as a margin driver ("AI-powered chatbots", "accelerated automation, notably through the increasing use of AI as a key optimization enabler"). It is simultaneously conceded as the reason clients may employ fewer people — the CEO's "future giants" line ("we have also, let's say, the future giants, the one who will take advantage of AI, in order to grow with them") is hope, not evidence. **AI cuts Pluxee's costs and may also cut its billable population. Only the first is in the guidance.**

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING.** This is no longer the company that listed in 2024. The revenue model — grow volumes, nudge the take rate up 50 basis points over four years — has been overwritten by regulation in its largest market, and management has responded by pivoting the equity story to margin, cash conversion, buybacks and bolt-on acquisitions. That pivot is being executed well. It is still a pivot.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** *the screener's premise for this name is arithmetically wrong, and correcting it removes most of the apparent margin of safety.* The 104% margin of safety, the 5.8x price-to-free-cash-flow and the 25.34 fair value are all built on a trailing earnings-per-share figure of 2.53 that double-counts two years of a semi-annual reporter, and on a 2.02B "net cash add-back" that is mostly client money the CFO has explicitly told the market not to count. On corrected numbers — trailing EPS ~1.42, recurring free cash flow ~417M, genuinely free excess cash a fraction of the headline — Pluxee at EUR 13.76 is *modestly* cheap against a peer group that has itself de-rated, not a 50-cent dollar. And the stock has already run: **+39% off its 52-week low of 9.905 and ~17% above its 50-day average of 11.81**, with 6% of that added on the 3 July 2026 relief print. The easy money in the fear was made by someone else in June.

**Economic moat: ERODING.**
- **Type:** primarily a **network** moat (a two-sided merchant/employer network in a near-duopoly with Edenred) layered on a **regulatory-license** moat (the PAT and its European equivalents are tax-privileged schemes that only accredited issuers may serve), with modest switching costs at the employer level.
- **Width, judged on the evidence, not the label:** returns are respectable but not fortress-grade — return on invested capital 10.6% (screener) to ~13.8% (trailing), return on equity flattered by a small equity base. Recurring earnings margin is *expanding* (+230bp, +229bp) — but that expansion is sourced to **cost cutting**, while the revenue-side rent is being taken away: gross margin is contracting (28.0%), the group take-up rate is down ~50 basis points, and volumes now grow 9.4% while revenue falls 3.3%. A moat you can only defend by cutting your own costs while your price is set by a ministry is not a wide one. **The decisive evidence is the 12 November 2026 interoperability mandate**: it does not squeeze the margin, it dismantles the closed loop that *is* the network. Rising margins on a legislated-down take rate is the signature of an eroding franchise, not a widening one.
- **Moat trend: ERODING.** Brazil's fee cap and interoperability, plus Italy's voucher-commission reform (which management says it "almost entirely absorbed" only by renegotiating client fees — i.e. by pushing the cost onto the other side of the network), are the same force arriving in two jurisdictions within eighteen months. There is no evidence in this file of the moat widening anywhere.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL — not terminal.**
The structural force is **payments disintermediation**: as benefit vouchers migrate onto open-loop rails (Brazil's 2% interchange arrangement, mandated interoperability, Google Pay/Apple Pay/QR acceptance), the economics converge toward ordinary card interchange, and the float — the third profit engine — is exposed both to falling rates and to any regulatory decision to shorten settlement, which Brazil has already done (15-day merchant reimbursement). Adjacent to this sits reimbursement-style compression: these are tax-subsidised schemes, and governments under budget pressure have shown, in Romania and Austria, that they will simply suspend them.

But **terminal** is the wrong word, and the evidence says so. Employee Benefits volumes still grow 8–9% organically; net retention is 99%, not 70%; face-value legal caps are *rising* across Europe, which mechanically grows the base; new client wins hit 92% of the annual target by Q3. The subsidised meal-benefit scheme is politically durable in France, Brazil, Italy and Turkey because it is popular with workers and cheap for treasuries relative to wage increases. What is happening is a **repricing of the rent, not the destruction of the demand**. Pluxee will be a smaller-take-rate business on a larger volume base.

**Fear-print or shrinking base?** **Partly a fear-print, but a small one, and it has already partially closed.** The base is not structurally shrinking — volumes grow — so this is not a classic value trap. But the discount is also not what the screen advertises: the peer anchor Edenred has de-rated on the *identical* regulatory shock to roughly 10x forward earnings and ~4x forward enterprise-value-to-earnings-before-interest-tax-depreciation-and-amortisation, so Pluxee's cheapness versus Edenred is shared sector beta on one unresolved driver, not idiosyncratic mispricing. **The honest read: a good business, honestly run, being repriced by a regulator, now trading at a modest discount to a de-rated peer after a 39% bounce — with its worst quarter pre-announced and its fiscal 2027 guidance still withheld.** Size for a repricing, not for a rescue, and do not pay up ahead of the late-October print.

bull_thesis:
Pluxee is the number-two player in a near-duopoly that sells employers tax-advantaged meal and lifestyle vouchers, and the operating engine underneath the headlines is running hot. In the quarter to May 2026, business volume issued grew 9.4% organically and Employee Benefits volumes grew 8.0%; by that same quarter the company had already booked EUR 1.2 billion of new annualised client volume, or 92% of its full-year target, with three months still to run. Demand is not the problem. Price is — and the price cut was imposed once, by one regulator, in one country.

The bull case rests on four legs. First, the margin engine is structural and proven. Recurring earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) margin expanded 230 basis points in fiscal 2025 against a 150-point plan, then another 229 basis points organically in the half to February 2026, reaching 37% — sourced to platform consolidation, product streamlining and automation rather than to one-off cuts. Management delivered that while revenue growth halved, which is the hard test. Second, cash conversion is genuinely excellent: 89% in fiscal 2025 and 86% in the recent half against a target of merely above 75%, and management responded to the beat by raising the commitment to above 80% rather than banking it. Free cash flow went from roughly EUR 290 million in fiscal 2023 to EUR 417 million in fiscal 2025.

Third, the Brazilian damage is turning out smaller than the market feared. On 3 July 2026 Pluxee reported quarterly revenue of EUR 312 million against roughly EUR 299 million expected, and organic revenue of −3.3% against a feared −4.3%; the shares rose 6% that day and full-year objectives were confirmed. Fourth — and this is the part the market is under-weighting — the growth drivers that survive the reform do not depend on employment growth. Legal caps on voucher face values are rising across Europe, mechanically lifting the volume base; the company banked EUR 2.9 billion of cumulative face-value uplift against a three-year target of EUR 3 billion with a year still to go. Small-business acquisition is now over 30% of new business, a mix that historically carries a better take rate. Acquisitions are compounding: Beneficio Facil drove more than 50% volume growth in Brazilian employee mobility in a single year.

Management quality is a real asset here and should be priced. They cut guidance five days after the Brazilian decree rather than drip-feeding it. When an analyst offered them the chance to call their reiterated guidance conservative in April 2026, the chief financial officer instead volunteered that second-half group margin would fall because of Brazil. That is a team that walks toward bad news. They also launched the company's first buyback, EUR 100 million, with the chief financial officer explicitly anchoring it to the share price: 'we are aware of where the stock price is currently trading, and versus the value we consider we are able to create from this company.'

What must hold for the bull case: Brazil's take-rate reset must prove to be a one-time step-down that laps by fiscal 2028 rather than the first of a sequence; the November 2026 interoperability mandate must not measurably shift merchant or employer share to open-loop card issuers; European face-value increases must keep offsetting soft employment; and float income — the interest Pluxee earns on client money held between issuing a voucher and paying the merchant — must not fall faster than operating profit grows. If those hold, a business compounding volumes at 8-9% with 37% margins and 86% cash conversion should not trade at roughly four times enterprise value to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, and a re-rating toward the high teens is straightforward arithmetic.
bear_thesis:
The bear case starts with a correction, not an opinion: the screening premise for this name is arithmetically wrong, and fixing it removes most of the advertised bargain. The scan reports trailing twelve-month earnings per share of 2.53 and free cash flow of EUR 540 million. Pluxee reports semi-annually, and the data feed labels those half-year periods as quarters — so summing 'four quarters' sums two full years. Real trailing earnings per share is roughly 1.42 (0.69 for the half to August 2025 plus 0.73 for the half to February 2026), and company-reported recurring free cash flow was EUR 417 million in fiscal 2025. The scan's 'Fair Value 25.34', 'Margin of Safety 104%', 'DCF fair value 77.7' and '5.8x price-to-free-cash-flow' are all computed on that doubled base. They are artefacts.

The second correction is the balance sheet. The input carries a EUR 2.02 billion net-cash 'add-back'. Most of that is float — client money owed onward to merchants, not shareholder property. Pluxee's own chief financial officer pre-emptively deflated exactly this reading in April 2026: 'it's worth differentiating 2 cash position... making a clear distinction between the contribution of float related cash to cash and this excess cash,' and then showed the two moving in opposite directions — 'this EUR 107 million improvement in the overall net cash position is the combination of EUR 140 million decrease in excess cash and EUR 240 million improvement overall on the float related [position].' Company-reported net financial cash at 28 February 2026 was about EUR 1.27 billion, and only a minority of that is genuinely free. Capitalising float interest income in the multiple and then adding the float cash back would count the same client money twice. The Altman-Z of 0.9 is likewise meaningless — a manufacturer's solvency score reading a benefits company's client float as crushing current liabilities.

With that cleared away, the real bear argument is the moat. Brazil's PAT reform (the tax-favoured meal-benefit scheme that underpins the group's largest market) capped the merchant discount rate at 3.6% from 10 February 2026, imposed 15-day merchant reimbursement, opened the system to a 2% interchange arrangement from 11 May 2026, and mandates full interoperability from 12 November 2026. The group take-up rate is already down about 50 basis points — which erases, in one decree, the entire 50-point improvement management spent four years earning. Volumes grew 9.4% while revenue fell 3.3% in the quarter to May 2026: that is the precise signature of price destruction. And interoperability is not a margin event, it is a franchise event — when the closed loop is opened by law, the merchant network that makes a Pluxee card worth more to an employer than a bank card becomes contestable by any card issuer. Italy has already run the same play on voucher commissions, which management says it absorbed 'almost entirely' only by renegotiating client fees, meaning it pushed the cost onto the other side of its own network. One regulator is a shock. Two in eighteen months is a trend, and Brazil's template is now written down for every other host government to copy.

The near-term picture is worse than the tape suggests. The worst quarter has been pre-announced and has not yet printed: 'In Q4, the impact will be somehow, in term of organic growth, twice the impact that we had in Q3 for Brazil' (chief financial officer, 3 July 2026). Fiscal 2027 guidance has been explicitly withheld as 'too early'. Net retention has already slipped to 99% against an above-100% objective, with the chief executive attributing it to end-user portfolios that 'turned negative' and to clients in automotive, information technology and staffing cutting budgets. Asked directly whether that was artificial-intelligence-driven hiring freezes, he answered: 'most of them are wondering what would be the future of their organization. Not many of them have very clear answers.' Pluxee's revenue is a levered bet on the number of employed people at its clients, and it has told the market its clients cannot forecast that number. Note the asymmetry management does not price: artificial intelligence is claimed repeatedly as a margin driver, and simultaneously conceded as the reason clients may employ fewer people. Only the first is in the guidance.

Three revenue lines have already been quietly pre-excused: Public Benefits (state programmes suspended or cut in Romania and Austria on budget grounds), the United Kingdom and the United States (being exited, 'less than 5% of group revenues', 'should return to a positive contribution from fiscal 2027'). Float income, the third profit engine, faces falling rates and a regulator that has already shortened settlement to 15 days in Brazil. And the shares are no longer washed out: at EUR 13.76 the stock sits 39% above its 52-week low of 9.905 and about 17% above its 50-day average of 11.81, having added 6% on the July relief print.

What confirms the bear case: fiscal 2027 guidance, when it lands, showing a second down year rather than a lap; measurable Brazilian volume or merchant share loss after 12 November 2026; any other host government (France, Italy, Turkey, Mexico) opening a fee-cap or interoperability consultation; net retention breaking below 98%; or float revenue turning negative as rates fall.
consensus_delta:
For a company screened as deep value, the honest finding is that the market is roughly right and our own screen is wrong. That is worth saying plainly, because the disagreement that matters here is with the input file, not with Wall Street.

Where the street is right and the screen is wrong: the scan claims a 104% margin of safety, a EUR 25.34 fair value, a EUR 77.70 discounted-cash-flow value and 5.8x price-to-free-cash-flow. Every one of those is computed on a trailing earnings-per-share figure of 2.53 that double-counts two years — Pluxee reports semi-annually and the feed labels half-years as quarters, so 0.73 + 0.69 + 0.67 + 0.44 sums twenty-four months, not twelve. Real trailing earnings per share is about 1.42. The 'TTM FCF 540M' has the same defect against company-reported recurring free cash flow of EUR 417m in fiscal 2025. And the EUR 2.02bn net-cash 'live correction' counts client float as shareholder property — the very error the chief financial officer went out of his way to pre-empt in April 2026 when he volunteered, unprompted, that the market should distinguish 'the contribution of float related cash' from 'excess cash', and then disclosed that excess cash FELL EUR 140m in the half. The street's Neutral consensus (3 buy, 9 hold, 2 sell; median target EUR 15.50) is, on corrected numbers, approximately correct.

Where we do disagree with the market, in two narrow places. First, the market is treating the Brazilian reform as a permanent impairment of the franchise when the evidence says it is a repricing of the rent on a growing base. Volumes tell the truth: business volume issued grew 9.4% organically in the quarter to May 2026 and Employee Benefits volumes 8.0%, while revenue fell 3.3%. Demand is intact; the meter was re-geared. Net retention is 99%, not 70%. New client wins hit 92% of the full-year target with a quarter to spare. Meal-benefit schemes are politically durable because they are popular with workers and cheap for treasuries relative to wage rises. Pluxee will be a lower-take-rate business on a bigger volume base — smaller, not dying. That argues the terminal value is not melting, and it is why the value case is held at moderate rather than written to a trap.

Second, and cutting the other way, the market is under-weighting interoperability. The sell-side conversation is almost entirely about the 3.6% merchant fee cap and the 15-day payment terms — margin arithmetic. The 12 November 2026 mandate that forces the closed loop open is a franchise question, not a margin question: once any card issuer can serve the accredited merchant network, the thing that makes a Pluxee card worth more to an employer than an ordinary bank card is contestable. Management frames payment-agnosticism as a feature ('fully payment agnostic, it integrates... Google Pay, Apple Pay, and QR code solutions'). It is the moat, described as a convenience. No analyst on either call pressed on this. If the street is wrong in a way that hurts, it is here — and it is the reason the moat is marked eroding and the value conviction capped, despite the optical cheapness.

Net: no exploitable expectations gap at EUR 13.76. The gap existed at EUR 9.905 in June and has largely closed.
forcing_function:
The late-October 2026 fiscal 2026 full-year results, which will carry the first fiscal 2027 guidance. That is the single event that resolves this name, and it is not a value-unlock — it is the removal of an unknown that could break either way.

The dated calendar, verified:
- 12 November 2025 — Brazilian presidential decree reforming the PAT scheme. Guidance cut five days later, 17 November 2025.
- 10 February 2026 — the 3.6% merchant discount rate cap and 15-day merchant reimbursement take effect. Fired.
- 11 May 2026 — market migration to an open-loop arrangement including a 2% interchange fee begins. Fired.
- 3 July 2026 — third-quarter revenue EUR 312m beats ~EUR 299m consensus; organic −3.3% beats the feared −4.3%; full-year objectives confirmed; shares +6%. Fired, and the re-rate it produced is spent.
- 12 November 2026 — full interoperability implementation and transition to a prepaid model for public-sector clients. Dated and binding by decree, but negative-skew: this is when the closed loop is forced open. It cannot pay you; it can only fail to hurt.
- Late October 2026 — fiscal 2026 results (fiscal year ends 31 August; the prior year's equivalent printed 30 October 2025). Fourth-quarter organic revenue at roughly twice the third quarter's Brazilian drag, per the chief financial officer on 3 July 2026, plus the first fiscal 2027 guide.

Why this is a soft, non-binding catalyst rather than a hard one, despite the real dates: nothing here is contractual and nothing pays out. The re-rating driver is a third party — the Brazilian government — whose reform is still unfolding in stages, and the shape is single-binary. There are no deal terms, no tender, no distribution, no announced asset sale. The value-unlock levers a special-situations investor would want have already been pulled and spent: the EUR 100m buyback is executed, the dividend is paid, and the spin-off itself was February 2024. What is left is a company waiting to find out what its regulator did to it, then telling us. That is a guidance event, not a forcing function.

Applying the current regime read directly: the regime rewards hard-dated catalysts inside the favourable window and penalises past or out-of-window ones — and the two events that could have re-rated this name (the buyback and the July beat) are both behind us and both fired, which is a down-rate. The regime favours structural special-situations in thin-coverage lanes and specifically ranks forced-sellers and spinoffs as the fattest lane this cycle; Pluxee's orphan window closed in 2024 and does not qualify. The regime deprioritises hard-binary single-driver theses, which is exactly the shape of a Brazilian regulatory outcome. Coverage is not thin — 14 analysts follow it.

One genuine regime credit, and it is worth stating because it is why this is not a pass: the regime prizes resolution-driver independence and warns hard against theses hinging on one shared macro factor. Pluxee is cleanly orthogonal to every dominant factor in the current book — the 24 July tariff cliff, the late-July artificial-intelligence capital-expenditure earnings test, the mid-August ceasefire clock, and the Federal Reserve path. Its driver is a Brazilian ministry. In a dispersion regime where single names re-rate violently on their own events and beta is dead, that independence has real portfolio value. But independence is a sizing virtue, not an entry signal, and it does not manufacture upside that the price does not offer. The caveat, per the peer file: this is independent of the macro book but NOT independent of Edenred — both move on the same unresolved regulatory driver.
valley_of_death:
The risky window is unusually well-signposted, because management signposted it themselves.

The dated event is the fiscal 2026 full-year result, due in late October 2026 (fiscal year ends 31 August; the prior year's equivalent was reported 30 October 2025). Two things land in that one print, both adverse or unknown:

1. The fourth quarter carries roughly twice the Brazilian drag of the third. The chief financial officer said so on 3 July 2026, verbatim: 'In Q4, the impact will be somehow, in term of organic growth, twice the impact that we had in Q3 for Brazil.' The third quarter printed −3.3% organic. So the fourth is likely in the range of −7% to −9% organic — the worst quarterly revenue number in the company's short public life, arriving as a headline.

2. Fiscal 2027 guidance, so far explicitly withheld — 'too early to provide detailed fiscal 2027 guidance' — should accompany it. This is the number that actually sets the stock, and nobody has it, including management. The full-year effect of the 3.6% fee cap, the 2% interchange leg that began 11 May 2026, and the interoperability regime starting 12 November 2026 all land inside fiscal 2027. On the adverse path this is a second consecutive down year, not a lap.

Between now and then, three further pressures:

- Float income is guided down in trajectory. Full-year float revenue growth is now expected to be only 'slightly positive' (3 July 2026), against a business that had been leaning on it. Falling rates and Brazil's shortened 15-day merchant settlement both work against it, and it is roughly a fifth of revenue at very high drop-through.

Net retention has already slipped to 99% from the above-100% objective. This is a slow leak, not a cliff, but it runs straight through the risky window.
- 12 November 2026 itself — full interoperability plus the transition to a prepaid model for public-sector clients — falls inside the window, before fiscal 2027 numbers can show whether it costs share.

What is NOT in the risky window, and this matters for sizing: there is no cash-burn hump, no maturity wall, no solvency question. The company generates roughly EUR 417m of recurring free cash flow, converts at 86-89%, and holds net financial cash of about EUR 1.27bn. The scan's Altman-Z of 0.9 is a false alarm — a manufacturer's solvency formula misreading a benefits company's client float as crushing current liabilities. This is a de-rating risk, not a distress risk. The stock can go to EUR 11 without the business being in any trouble at all.
positioning_washout:
There is no mechanical forced-selling dynamic available here, and pretending otherwise would be the easy mistake.

The spin-off orphan window — the one genuinely mechanical event in this name's life — is long gone. Pluxee separated from Sodexo and listed in February 2024. The index reshuffling, the Sodexo-holder distribution overhang and the forced flow from mandates that could not hold the stub all cleared through 2024. The screener's radar reached for exactly this — 'a spin-off orphan-stock discount... still working through ownership/index overhang' — and it is more than two years stale. This is not a live forced-seller setup, and it should not be scored as one against a regime read that ranks forced-sellers and spinoffs as the fattest lane. Pluxee does not belong in that lane.

There is no dividend cut to flush a yield-focused base either. The dividend is small and rising — EUR 0.38 per share for fiscal 2025, up 9%, roughly EUR 55m in total, on a stock at EUR 13.76. That is a sub-3% yield. No income mandate holds this for the payout, so no income mandate is forced out of it.

What actually happened to the shareholder base is the opposite of a washout, and it is the timing problem. The capitulation already occurred and has already been bought. The stock bottomed at EUR 9.905 within the last 52 weeks, and at EUR 13.76 it now sits 39% above that low and roughly 17% above its 50-day average of EUR 11.81 — a 200-day average of EUR 12.42 that price has now crossed and left behind, up 8% against it. The single clearest marker: shares rose 6% on 3 July 2026 when third-quarter revenue of EUR 312m beat the ~EUR 299m consensus and organic −3.3% beat the feared −4.3%. The fear print was bought in June by someone else. The weak hands are out; what remains is a Neutral-rated holder base (3 buy, 9 hold, 2 sell across 14 analysts) that has already survived the worst headline and is waiting, exactly as we are, for the fiscal 2027 guide.

One live technical pressure, and it works against a buyer: the company's own EUR 100m buyback is essentially spent — it was a fiscal 2025 programme, executed through the half to February 2026, and it is a named contributor to the EUR 140m decline in excess cash that half. The marginal price-insensitive bid that supported the stock through the sell-off has been withdrawn. Management has since redirected the priority to acquisitions — 'M&A remains a key pillar of our growth strategy' — rather than committing to a follow-on repurchase.

The mirror image is the real risk: if the late-October print pairs a −7% to −9% fourth quarter with a soft or absent fiscal 2027 guide, the mechanical selling comes from index and quality-factor funds re-screening a second consecutive down year, not from anyone capitulating on fear. That would be the flush worth buying.
moderator_conclusion:
Pass on the entry, keep the name, and wait for late October. The business is good and the price is no longer.

The first duty here is to correct the file, because the case for owning Pluxee was built on arithmetic that does not survive contact. The screen advertises a 104% margin of safety, a EUR 25.34 fair value and 5.8x price-to-free-cash-flow. Those rest on trailing earnings per share of 2.53, which double-counts two years — Pluxee reports semi-annually and the data feed labels half-years as quarters, so the 'four quarters' summed are twenty-four months. Real trailing earnings per share is about 1.42. The EUR 2.02bn net-cash add-back is worse: most of it is float, client money owed onward to merchants, and Pluxee's own chief financial officer volunteered the distinction unprompted in April 2026 precisely to stop people making this mistake — then disclosed that genuinely free excess cash FELL EUR 140m in the half, spent on the dividend and the buyback. Company-reported net financial cash was about EUR 1.27bn, of which only a slice is shareholder property. Corrected, the sum-of-the-parts base case is EUR 15.00, not EUR 25. The stock closed at EUR 13.76 on 16 July 2026. That is roughly 9% of upside to fair value, against 20% of downside to the adverse case at EUR 11.00. The asymmetry points the wrong way.

The second duty is to be honest about what happened to the price. This was a genuine opportunity at EUR 9.905, and 39% of it has been taken — by someone else, in June and early July. The shares now trade 17% above their 50-day average and 8% above their 200-day, having added 6% on 3 July 2026 when third-quarter revenue beat and Brazil proved less bad than feared. The relief trade fired. The buyback that provided a price-insensitive bid through the sell-off is spent, and management has redirected the next euro to acquisitions rather than committing to a follow-on. Buying now is paying up for a thesis whose cheap entry has already closed.

The third duty is to say what is genuinely good, because it is why this is a wait and not a pass-forever. Management is the best asset in the file. They cut guidance five days after the Brazilian decree. When an analyst handed them an excuse to call their reiterated guidance conservative, they instead volunteered that second-half margin would fall. They set a 150-basis-point margin target and delivered 230, then raised the cash-conversion floor rather than bank the beat. Underneath the regulatory headline the engine is running: business volumes +9.4% organic, Employee Benefits volumes +8.0%, 92% of the annual new-client target booked with a quarter to spare, net retention 99%. Volumes up while revenue falls is price destruction, not demand destruction — and that distinction is the whole difference between a repricing and a value trap. Meal-benefit schemes are politically durable; Brazil re-geared the meter, it did not close the market.

But the moat is eroding, and that caps how much this can be paid for. The group take-up rate is already down about 50 basis points — erasing, in one decree, the entire 50 points management spent four years earning. Margins are expanding only because costs are being cut, while the price is set by a ministry. And the 12 November 2026 interoperability mandate is the leg nobody on either call pressed on: it does not squeeze the margin, it forces open the closed loop that IS the network. Management describes payment-agnosticism as a feature. It is the franchise, described as a convenience. Italy already ran the same play and was absorbed only by pushing the cost onto the other side of the network. Two jurisdictions in eighteen months, with the template now written down for the rest. That is why the moat reads eroding, why the value conviction is capped at 3, and why the honest cheapness — a modest discount to a de-rated Edenred at ~10.3x forward earnings and ~4.1x forward enterprise-value-to-earnings — is shared sector beta on one unresolved regulator, not single-name alpha. The peer file is right and the radar was wrong: Edenred is not a 20-25x comparable any more, and the discount to it is mostly justified by Pluxee's heavier Brazil weight.

The regime read pushes the same direction. Both catalysts that could have re-rated this name are behind us and spent. The spin-off orphan window closed in February 2024, so this does not belong in the forced-seller lane the regime currently ranks fattest. Coverage is not thin — 14 analysts, Neutral consensus, median target EUR 15.50, which corroborates our EUR 15.00 almost exactly. The remaining driver is a third-party, single-binary regulatory outcome, precisely the shape the regime deprioritises. The one real regime credit is independence: Pluxee's fate turns on a Brazilian ministry, cleanly orthogonal to the tariff cliff, the artificial-intelligence capital-expenditure test, the ceasefire clock and the Fed. In a dispersion regime that is worth something — but it is a sizing virtue, not an entry signal, and it buys no upside the price does not offer.

So: wait for the flush, and the flush has a date. Late October 2026 brings the fiscal 2026 full-year result carrying a fourth quarter with roughly twice the third quarter's Brazilian drag — call it −7% to −9% organic, the worst headline in the company's public life — alongside the first fiscal 2027 guidance, which management has so far refused to give. That guide is the number that sets the stock, and nobody has it. If it lands soft and the index and quality-factor screens re-rate a second consecutive down year, the mechanical selling that follows is the entry, not the June fear. If it laps clean, we pay up a little for certainty and still make the arithmetic work toward EUR 19.75 on the favourable path. Either way, there is no reason to own it into a pre-announced bad print with 9% of upside and no floor beneath the stock — the balance-sheet cash cannot be leaned on, because it belongs to somebody else. Wait for the fiscal 2027 guide.

interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — Pluxee N.V. (PLX.PA, Euronext Paris)

*Prepared 2026-07-17. Price used throughout: **EUR 13.76** (Euronext Paris close, 2026-07-16, via FMP live quote). All figures in euros unless stated. Pluxee's fiscal year ends 31 August, so "H1 fiscal 2026" means September 2025 through February 2026, and "Q3 fiscal 2026" means March through May 2026.*

Pluxee is the employee-benefits business Sodexo spun off and listed separately in February 2024. It issues meal and lifestyle vouchers (increasingly digital cards and an app) that employers buy for their staff, and it earns money three ways: a fee from the employer, a commission from the merchant who accepts the voucher, and interest on the large pool of client money it holds between issuing a voucher and paying the merchant — what the industry calls the "float". It operates in 28 countries; Latin America (overwhelmingly Brazil) and Continental Europe are roughly 40% and 44% of operating revenue.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

**The story has quietly changed shape over the last nine months, from "low-double-digit growth compounder" to "cost and cash machine absorbing a regulatory reset."**

At the fiscal 2025 results call (30 October 2025), the framing was unambiguously offensive. Aurélien Sonet led with "another very strong year, in which we executed our strategy with discipline and delivered above expectations across all key metrics" — 10.6% organic revenue growth, recurring earnings margin up 230 basis points against a 150-point plan, 89% cash conversion against a target of "above 75%". The capital-allocation news was a flex, not a defence: a raised dividend of EUR 0.38 per share plus a first-ever EUR 100 million buyback, which the CFO explicitly tied to the share price — "we are aware of where the stock price is currently trading, and versus the value we consider we are able to create from this company."

Thirteen days later, on 12 November 2025, the Brazilian government issued the decree reforming the PAT (Programa de Alimentação do Trabalhador — the tax-favoured meal-benefit scheme that is the economic basis of Pluxee's largest market). Pluxee cut its fiscal 2026 guidance on 17 November 2025. That single external event is the hinge of the whole arc.

By the H1 fiscal 2026 call (16 April 2026), the vocabulary had inverted. Growth was no longer the lead — margin was: "profitability delivered ahead of plan", "operating leverage embedded in our business model", "the strong execution of our efficiency initiatives", "cost discipline has become an increasingly important margin driver". Organic revenue growth had halved to 5.6%. The agenda itself now carried a dedicated item — "an update on the regulatory situation in Brazil" — that did not exist a year earlier.

Two growth drivers were quietly demoted along the way. **Public Benefits** (state-funded programmes) went from a proof point in October 2025 to a euphemism by April 2026 — "the effects related to the contract cycle and order phasing, which are inherent in this business" — after the CFO had already conceded in October that "some countries, especially in Western Europe, like Romania or Austria... decisions were taken by the state, and because of some budget constraints, to suspend or to reduce some of these programs." **Net retention** slid from a headline achievement ("we maintained a net retention rate of 100%, in line with our midterm objective") to a hedge ("net retention proved resilient despite a more challenging macro environment"), and by Q3 fiscal 2026 it had printed **99%** — below the stated above-100% objective.

Two drivers were promoted to carry the load: **face value increases** (legal caps on voucher values rising across Europe, plus Latin American inflation) and **acquisitions** (Beneficio Fácil, Cobee, Skipr, the Santander partnership). Both are real. Both are also, notably, drivers that do not require the underlying employed population to grow — which matters, because that is precisely what stopped growing.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

**Before the table, three corrections to the screener block that the director must see, because two of them invert the headline conclusion.**

| Screener field | What it says | What is actually true | Why it is wrong |
|---|---|---|---|
| **TTM diluted EPS** | **2.53** | **≈ 1.42** | Pluxee reports semi-annually. The data feed labels those half-year periods "Q2" and "Q4", so summing "four quarters" (0.73 + 0.69 + 0.67 + 0.44) sums **two full years**. Real trailing-twelve-month earnings per share = H2 fiscal 2025 (0.69) + H1 fiscal 2026 (0.73) = **1.42**. |
| **TTM FCF 540M** | 540M | **≈ 417M** (fiscal 2025 recurring free cash flow, company-reported); H1 fiscal 2026 recurring free cash flow was 210M | Same double-count mechanic. Management's own figure: "our free cash flow engine has expanded very materially from circa EUR 290 million in fiscal 2023 to EUR 417 million in fiscal 2025." |
| **Net cash 2.02B** ("a genuine SoP add-back") | 2.02B | Company-reported **net financial cash of ~1.27B** at 28 February 2026 — and only a *minority slice* of that is genuinely free | This is the single most important correction. Most of Pluxee's cash is **float** — money that belongs to clients and is owed to merchants. Management draws the line themselves: "it's worth differentiating 2 cash position. You have the overall net cash position. And we also disclosed... what we call this net excess cash position, making a clear distinction between the contribution of float related cash to cash and this excess cash." They then showed the two moving in *opposite* directions in H1 fiscal 2026: "this EUR 107 million improvement in the overall net cash position is the combination of EUR 140 million **decrease in excess cash** and EUR 240 million improvement overall on the float related [position]." Treating 2.02B as a shareholder add-back would count client money twice — once as cash on the balance sheet and again as the float interest income capitalised in the earnings multiple. |

Knock-on: the screener's "Fair Value 25.34 / Margin of Safety 104%", "DCF fair value 77.7" and "P/FCF 5.8x" are all computed off the doubled earnings and cash-flow base. **They are artefacts, not signals.** The Altman-Z of 0.9 is equally meaningless here — a solvency score built for manufacturers reads a benefits company's client float as crushing current liabilities.

**Now the claims themselves.**

| Management claim | Where | The hard evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Robust margin expansion... underscoring the operating leverage of our model" | FY25 + H1 FY26 | Recurring earnings margin +230bp in fiscal 2025 (vs +150bp planned), then +229bp organically in H1 fiscal 2026 to 37%; recurring earnings +12.9% organic on +5.6% revenue. Reported net income 68M (H2 FY24) → 100M (H2 FY25) → 105M (H1 FY26). | **Corroborated.** The strongest, cleanest claim in the file. |
| "Outstanding cash generation and conversion" | FY25 | 89% recurring cash conversion vs a ">75% average" target; 86% in H1 fiscal 2026; free cash flow 290M (FY23) → 417M (FY25). | **Corroborated**, once the feed's doubled 540M is discarded. |
| "Strong momentum in new client acquisition" | Every call | EUR 1.5B of new annualised business volume in fiscal 2025 vs a 1.3B target; a record 0.9B in H1 fiscal 2026; 1.2B by Q3 = 92% of the full-year target with a quarter to run; business volume issued +9.4% organic in Q3 fiscal 2026. | **Corroborated — and this is the tell.** Volumes are *growing high-single-digit while revenue shrinks*. The problem is not demand. It is price, imposed by regulators. |
| "We maintained a net retention rate of 100%, in line with our midterm objective" | FY25 | Printed **99% in Q3 fiscal 2026** — below the above-100% target. The CEO had already conceded the cause: end-user portfolio contribution "turned negative" in H2 fiscal 2025. | **Diverging.** Not yet broken, but the claim has lapsed and the driver is deteriorating, not stabilising. |
| "Consensus fwd EPS growth +0.4%" (screener) vs "we remain deeply committed to establishing Pluxee as a sustainably profitable growth group" | FY25 close | The street models roughly flat earnings. Q3 fiscal 2026 organic revenue **−3.3%**; management guides Q4's Brazil drag at "twice the impact that we had in Q3". | **Narrative is richer than the trajectory.** The words still say growth compounder; the numbers say two years of flat-to-down revenue while a regulator resets the take rate. |
| "Beat 1 of 5 quarters (20%)" (screener) | — | Against *revenue* consensus Pluxee has been closer than that: Q3 fiscal 2026 revenue of 312M beat the ~299M consensus and organic −3.3% beat the −4.3% feared (3 July 2026). | **Screener metric is unreliable for a semi-annual reporter** and should not be leaned on. |

**The core forensic finding:** the operational claims are true and the accounting is clean. What is *not* true is the screener's premise that this is a 5.8x free-cash-flow, 104%-margin-of-safety orphan. Strip the double-count and the float, and Pluxee is a well-run, modestly-levered duopolist whose regulator is legislating its take rate down — trading at a *modest*, not spectacular, discount.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Declining** — from confident-offensive to confident-defensive. The confidence is intact; the *subject* of the confidence has moved from revenue to costs.

- **FY25 (30 Oct 2025) — offensive.** "Delivered above expectations across all key metrics"; "we are clearly well ahead of our initial plan"; "a step change in the group's financial profile". Even the buyback was framed as conviction: "this is a very good sign of our confidence in the Pluxee potential."
- **FY25, under questioning — the first crack.** Pressed by Barclays on the Q4 slowdown, the CFO named it: state programmes "suspend[ed] or... reduce[d]" in Romania and Austria, "weighing at least temporarily, and we'll see further on our organic growth." That "we'll see further" is the only unhedged moment of uncertainty in the October call.
- **H1 FY26 (16 Apr 2026) — defensive, but specific.** "Solid", "resilient", "on track" replace "outstanding" and "above expectations". The framing is explicitly about withstanding: "allows us to enter H2 from a position of strength amid a more uncertain macro and geopolitical environment."
- **H1 FY26, the Brazil answer — the most important tonal moment.** Asked by UBS whether the reiterated earnings guidance implied conservatism, the CFO instead pre-announced a decline: "we expect all the regions to go on improving the EBITDA margin... with one exception, one big exception, which is going to be Brazil... the reform for the short term and for the second half of the year will weigh a lot on the EBITDA margin of the group... in the second half of the year, we will face a lower EBITDA margin compared to the previous year." That is a management team walking *toward* the bad news, unprompted, on the record. It is a credibility asset.
- **Q3 FY26 (3 Jul 2026) — clinical.** Guidance confirmed; the Q4 hit quantified in advance ("twice the impact that we had in Q3"); fiscal 2027 guidance explicitly withheld as "too early".

Guidance has become *more* specific over time, not less — the opposite of the usual deterioration pattern. But specificity is now being spent describing decline.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High.**

| Guided | When | Delivered | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Low double-digit" organic revenue growth, FY25 | FY24 | +10.6% organic | Met |
| ~+150bp recurring margin expansion, FY25 | FY24 | **+230bp** | Beat materially |
| ">75% average" cash conversion, FY24–26 | FY24 | 89% (FY25), 86% (H1 FY26) | Beat, then *raised* the commitment to ">80% average" |
| EUR 1.3B annual new-client business volume | FY25 | EUR 1.5B | Beat |
| EUR 3B cumulative face-value uplift over 3 years | FY24 | 2.9B reached by H1 FY26 (year 2 of 3) | On track / early |
| FY26 objectives *as revised 17 Nov 2025* (stable organic revenue, slight margin expansion, ~80% cash conversion) | Nov 2025 | Confirmed at H1 (Apr) and again at Q3 (Jul); 9-month revenue +2.7% organic | Tracking |

**No sandbagging pattern in the ordinary sense — the reverse.** They set a 150bp margin target and delivered 230bp, then raised the cash-conversion floor rather than bank the beat. The one guidance cut (17 November 2025) came **five days** after the Brazilian decree — immediate, not delayed, not drip-fed. When they had a chance to hide behind "conservatism" on the April call, they instead volunteered that H2 group margin would fall.

The screener's "beat 1/5 quarters (20%)" contradicts this and should be disregarded: Pluxee reports twice a year and gives revenue-only updates in Q1/Q3, so a quarterly EPS-beat count is measuring noise. The Q3 fiscal 2026 print (3 July 2026) beat both revenue and organic-growth consensus.

**One genuine reservation:** the fiscal 2027 guide has been deferred. Management called it "too early to provide detailed fiscal 2027 guidance" given "ongoing regulatory uncertainty". Their credibility is high *on things they have guided*. The number that matters most to the stock right now is the one they have not yet given.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **"What are you doing with the cash?" — asked repeatedly, never fully answered.** Deutsche Bank's André Juillard (H1 FY26): "Your cash net position is even stronger than what it was at the end of last year. Do you have any new plan about the use of this cash or still not clear?" The answer was the float/excess-cash distinction plus "M&A remains a key pillar... we'll come back to you when it will be." The same analyst had already needled them in October — "as a summary, the message is step by step" — and the CFO's reply, "As always," is the tell. **Analysts do not believe the cash pile is as available as it looks, and management has not shown them the excess-cash bridge in a way that settles it.** This is the pressure point that later turned into the buyback.
- **Net retention decomposition — deflected twice.** Bernstein's Sabrina Blanc pushed on where retention deteriorated; the answer named "the evolution of the end user portfolio" but gave no numbers. She then asked directly for the non-meal-voucher share of revenue and got only: "the contribution coming from the cross-selling in percentage is higher than the overall growth." **A ratio in place of a number.** The multi-benefit diversification story — the strategic answer to meal-voucher regulatory risk — is unquantified.
- **The Q4 fiscal 2025 order postponement — asked, answered vaguely, then confirmed as real.** Barclays' Pravin Gondhale asked for the size of the postponed European public programmes. The CFO: "I don't have in mind the impact in terms of basis points." Six months later Public Benefits weakness in Continental Europe was a named drag, and by Q3 fiscal 2026 Continental Europe operating revenue was **−1.5% over nine months**. The non-answer preceded the bad news.
- **The AI question analysts are asking and management cannot answer.** UBS's Mahir Bidani (H1 FY26) asked whether client headcount reductions were "because of AI fears and then stopping hiring". The CEO's answer was candid to a fault: "most of them are wondering what would be the future of their organization. **Not many of them have very clear answers.**" He then named automotive, IT and staffing as under pressure. **Pluxee's revenue is a levered bet on the number of employed people at its clients** — and it has just told the market that its clients do not know what that number will be.
- **What analysts are not pressing on, and should be: interoperability.** The Brazil discussion is framed as a merchant-fee cap and payment terms. The 12 November 2026 milestone — full interoperability, forcing the closed-loop network open — is the leg that attacks the *moat*, not the margin. It gets far less airtime than the 3.6% fee cap.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The take rate is being legislated down.** Brazil's PAT reform capped the merchant discount rate at 3.6% (effective 10 February 2026), imposed 15-day merchant reimbursement, opened the system to a 2% interchange arrangement (11 May 2026) and mandates full interoperability from 12 November 2026. Group take-up rate is already down ~50 basis points. Management's own 4-year brag — "we have improved our take rate of 50 basis points" over four years (FY25 call) — has been erased by one decree.

🔴 **Volumes up, revenue down — the definition of price destruction.** Q3 fiscal 2026: business volume issued **+9.4%** organic, Employee Benefits volume **+8.0%**, and total revenue **−3.3%** organic. The engine is running; the meter has been re-geared.

🔴 **Net retention broke below the objective** — 99% in Q3 fiscal 2026 against an above-100% target, with the CEO attributing it to end-user portfolios that "turned negative" (H2 fiscal 2025) and to clients in automotive, IT and staffing "reading [reducing] some of their budgets".

🔴 **The worst quarter is still ahead and pre-announced.** "In Q4, the impact will be somehow, in term of organic growth, twice the impact that we had in Q3 for Brazil" (CFO, 3 July 2026). Fiscal 2027 guidance withheld.

🔴 **The cash is not what the screen thinks it is.** See §2. Excess cash *fell* EUR 140 million in H1 fiscal 2026.

🔴 **Insider buy ratio 0.00** — while the *company* bought EUR 100 million of stock, no individual insider did.

🟢 **Management pre-announced its own bad news, twice.** Guidance cut five days after the Brazilian decree (17 November 2025); H2 margin decline volunteered in answer to a question about *conservatism* (16 April 2026). This is not a promotional team.

🟢 **Margin expansion is structural, not cosmetic** — +230bp (FY25) and +229bp organic (H1 FY26), sourced to platform consolidation, product-range streamlining and automation, and delivered while revenue growth halved. The efficiency programme is doing exactly what it claimed.

🟢 **Commercial engine is genuinely strong** — 92% of the full-year new-client target achieved with a quarter remaining; small-business acquisition now >30% of new business, which is the mix that historically carries a better take rate.

🟢 **Brazil came in less bad than feared** — Q3 organic −3.3% vs −4.3% consensus, revenue 312M vs ~299M expected; shares +6% on 3 July 2026.

🟢 **Geographic and driver diversification is real** — 28 countries, three regions, face-value legal-cap increases across Europe providing a mechanical volume tailwind independent of employment.

🟢 **The capital-allocation policy moved from words to cash** — first buyback (EUR 100 million) plus a 9% dividend increase, with the CFO explicitly anchoring it to the depressed share price.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **The float/excess-cash distinction is now volunteered, not extracted.** In October 2025 the cash story was "significant increases in our net cash position". By April 2026 the CFO opens with "it's worth differentiating 2 cash position" *before* being pressed. **Management is pre-emptively deflating a balance-sheet number the market was over-reading.** When a CFO volunteers that his cash is smaller than it looks, believe him — and note that the screener's 2.02B add-back is exactly the error he is trying to head off.
- **"Sustainably profitable growth group" replaced "low double-digit growth".** In October 2025 the objective was a number. By April 2026 the closing line is an adjective. The quantified ambition has been retired without ever being formally withdrawn.
- **A new voice with a different register.** The Q3 fiscal 2026 call (3 July 2026) was fronted on the Brazil question by CFO **Stéphane Abrioux**, not Stéphane Lhopiteau. The tonal shift is notable: where Lhopiteau spent paragraphs contextualising, Abrioux quantified the coming damage in one sentence — "twice the impact that we had in Q3". A cleaner, colder communication style, which usually accompanies an internal decision to stop defending the old growth frame.
- **"Highly selective" is doing quiet work.** Public Benefits is now always accompanied by "our highly selective approach" and "sustainably accretive to growth and profitability" — the language of a business being shrunk on purpose, pre-justified. Same with the UK and US: "progressively exiting noncore, lower return activities", "less than 5% of group revenues", "should return to a positive contribution from fiscal 2027". Three separate revenue lines have been pre-excused.
- **Interoperability is being discussed as a payments feature, not as the end of the moat.** The FY25 call sells payment-agnosticism as a *strength* — "being fully payment agnostic, it integrates the most popular digital payment options such as Google Pay, Apple Pay, and QR code solutions". That is the same force Brazil is about to mandate. When the closed loop is opened by law, the merchant network — the thing that makes a Pluxee card worth more to an employer than a bank card — becomes contestable by any card issuer. **Management frames this as convenience. It is the moat.**
- **AI appears on both sides of the ledger, and management only counts one.** AI is repeatedly claimed as a margin driver ("AI-powered chatbots", "accelerated automation, notably through the increasing use of AI as a key optimization enabler"). It is simultaneously conceded as the reason clients may employ fewer people — the CEO's "future giants" line ("we have also, let's say, the future giants, the one who will take advantage of AI, in order to grow with them") is hope, not evidence. **AI cuts Pluxee's costs and may also cut its billable population. Only the first is in the guidance.**
